content: 1. Middleton et al. (2015) and Carducci et al. (2021) conducted systematic reviews on the effects of zinc supplementation during pregnancy. Their findings, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, suggest that zinc supplementation may improve pregnancy and infant outcomes, though the evidence is derived from studies with moderate risk of bias and design limitations. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations on antenatal care to promote a positive pregnancy experience. These guidelines emphasize evidence-based practices to improve maternal and perinatal health outcomes. 3. Vogel et al. (2019) described the development and application of a living guidelines approach for WHO recommendations on maternal and perinatal health. 4. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (second edition) outlines the processes for creating evidence-based recommendations. This includes the use of the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) framework to assess the quality of evidence. 5. Downe et al. (2016) conducted a scoping review to identify the processes and outcomes of antenatal care that are most important to healthy pregnant women. Their findings highlight the need for care that is respectful, individualized, and supportive. 6. Downe et al. (2019) also synthesized qualitative evidence on the provision and uptake of routine antenatal services. Their review, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, underscores the importance of addressing barriers to accessing care. 7. The WHO has developed a standardized toolkit to help countries adapt antenatal care recommendations to their specific contexts. This toolkit, described by Barreix et al. (2020), provides a structured approach to guideline adaptation. 8. The WHO Steering Group and external experts, including representatives from various regions and organizations, contributed to the development of these guidelines. Their expertise spans maternal and perinatal health, nutrition, and implementation research. 9. The GRADE tables for zinc supplementation evaluate the evidence for its use in pregnant women. The findings indicate that while zinc supplementation may reduce adverse outcomes, the evidence is limited by inconsistency, imprecision, and moderate risk of bias in the included studies. 10. The WHO emphasizes the importance of a healthy diet during pregnancy, as outlined in their fact sheets and publications. Adequate nutrition is critical for maternal and infant health. 11. The UNICEF Supply Catalogue provides resources to support maternal and child health programs globally, ensuring access to essential supplies. 12. The guideline development process involved a diverse group of experts, including obstetricians, gynecologists, nutritionists, and public health professionals. 13. The evidence on zinc supplementation highlights the need for further research to address gaps and improve the quality of data. This includes addressing inconsistencies and limitations in study design. 14. The WHO Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health, along with other stakeholders, continues to work on improving global health outcomes through evidence-based guidelines and interventions.
